title: Last_Mile_(artificial_intelligence)
summary:
The last mile in artificial intelligence refers to the critical final stage of taking AI systems from development to real-world deployment and impact. The term is borrowed from logistics, where it describes the final and most challenging leg of delivery. When machine learning engineers and data scientists refer to the last mile, they reference the steps required to take an AI solution and make it available for generalized, widespread use.

There are three broad stages in the development of data-driven technologies like machine learning. In the first mile, data are acquired, labeled, and preprocessed. The middle mile focuses on developing and testing technical performance of different algorithms. Only in the last mile are algorithms embedded in real-world processes and tested for impact on real-world outcomes. With less than half of AI projects ever reaching a production win, optimizing the processes that comprise the last mile would unlock significant innovation.

For AI to move from a few generalist systems to the myriad of specialized systems needed for deployment throughout the economy, an enormous amount of costly last mile customization is needed. While 80% of computer vision tasks are technically feasible to automate, after accounting for last-mile costs only 23% of worker tasks are both technically feasible and cost effective to automate. The last-mile customizations needed to use AI across diverse business applications drive up costs, substantially changing the economics of adoption.

Although much effort is focused on improving the technical performance of artificial intelligence, there are compelling reasons to focus more on implementation. In this last mile of implementation lie many complex challenges that may make technically high-performing systems perform poorly in practice. Implementation should be seen as an agile, iterative, and lightweight process of obtaining training data, developing algorithms, and crafting these into tools and workflows.
